pages.c14-p01: Explain what a network is, why computers are networked, and the difference between a LAN and a WAN
pages.c14-p02: Identify the main pieces of network hardware and describe what each one does
pages.c14-p03: Compare wired and wireless connections, including Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and choose a suitable one for a task
pages.c14-p04: Describe star, bus and mesh network topologies and give an advantage and a disadvantage of each
pages.c14-p05: Compare client-server and peer-to-peer networks and decide which is suitable for a given situation
pages.c14-p06: Explain how data is split into packets and sent across a network using packet switching
pages.c14-p07: Explain what IP addresses and MAC addresses are and the difference between them
pages.c14-p08: Describe, step by step, what happens when you type a URL into a browser, including the role of DNS
pages.c14-p09: Explain bandwidth and network speed units, and calculate how long a file will take to download
pages.c14-p10: Explain what the cloud and the Internet of Things are, and evaluate their benefits and risks

q.q: Which is the best definition of a computer network?
o: A program that finds and removes viruses from computers
A single computer with a very large amount of storage space
A type of web browser used to visit sites on the internet
Two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources
q.why: A network needs at least two connected devices.

q.q: Which of these is an example of a LAN?
o: The computers in your school
The internet
A bank linking branches in five countries
A satellite TV service
q.why: One school site is a small area, so it is a LAN.

q.q: Which of these is a drawback of joining computers in a network?
o: Users can log on from any computer in school
Printers can be shared by everyone in the room
Work can be backed up centrally in one go
Viruses can spread from one computer to others
q.why: Being connected means malware can travel between computers.

q.q: Which is the biggest wide area network in the world?
o: The internet
Bluetooth
The school network
Wi-Fi
q.why: The internet links millions of networks worldwide.

q.q: Why can you open your work from any computer in the school?
o: It is stored on the printer, which every computer shares
It is saved on your own USB stick automatically
It is copied onto every computer in the school each night
It is saved on a server, not on the computer in front of you
q.why: Networks let work be saved centrally.

q.q: Thirty pupils share one printer instead of having thirty. Which benefit of networking is this?
o: Central management
Communication
Sharing files
Sharing hardware
q.why: Networks let devices share hardware.

q.q: If the main server goes down, nobody can get to their files. What is this drawback called?
o: Hacking from outside
Single point of failure
Cost of equipment
Need for expertise
q.why: Everyone depends on the server.

q.q: Who usually owns the equipment in a WAN?
o: It is usually rented from telecoms companies
Nobody owns it, as it is all wireless
Each user owns their own part of it
The organisation itself, such as the school
q.why: A LAN's equipment is owned by the organisation.

q.q: A bank links all of its branches across the UK. What type of network is this?
o: Stand-alone
LAN
Peer-to-peer
WAN
q.why: It covers a large area.

q.q: Which device links the school's LAN to the outside world?
o: Hub
NIC
Router
Switch
q.why: Routers connect different networks together.

q.q: What does a switch do?
o: Converts digital data into signals for a phone line or cable
Connects the school network to other networks such as the internet
Gives every device its own unique MAC address when it is made
Connects devices within a LAN and sends data to the correct device
q.why: A switch works inside one network.

q.q: In what form does data travel along a fibre optic cable?
o: As radio waves through the air
As pulses of light in glass
As electrical signals in copper
As sound waves along a tube
q.why: Fibre uses light, so it is fast and unaffected by electrical interference.

q.q: A smart TV must have which piece of hardware to join any network?
o: A modem
A NIC
A printer
A fibre optic cable
q.why: Without a NIC a device cannot connect to any network.

q.q: What does a modem do?
o: Lets wireless devices join a wired network using Wi-Fi
Sends data only to the device in the LAN it is meant for
Converts digital data into signals for a phone line or cable, and back
Stores everyone's files and controls who can open them
q.why: Modem is short for modulator demodulator.

q.q: What does a wireless access point do?
o: Converts light into electrical signals
Connects the school to the internet
Lets wireless devices join a wired network
Gives each device a MAC address
q.why: WAPs are often the white boxes on classroom ceilings.

q.q: Which memory aid is correct?
o: A switch works within a network; a router works between networks
A router works within a network; a switch works between networks
A switch and a router both only work within one network
A modem works within a network; a NIC works between networks
q.why: Switch = within; router = between.

q.q: What does a router use to forward packets towards their destination?
o: IP addresses
Domain names
Packet trailers
MAC addresses
q.why: Switches use MAC addresses within a LAN.

q.q: Which devices are usually inside a home broadband 'router' box?
o: Only a NIC and a long Ethernet cable
A file server, a print server and a hub
Router, switch, wireless access point and often a modem
A router and a printer, but nothing else
q.why: Schools use separate, bigger devices for each job.

q.q: Why would a school use fibre optic cable to link two buildings far apart?
o: It is affected by electrical interference
It is cheaper and easier to fit than copper
It carries data very fast over many kilometres
It can only carry data up to 100 metres
q.why: Ethernet copper only reaches about 100 m.

q.q: Why did switches replace hubs?
o: A hub only works with wireless devices
A hub cannot connect more than two devices together
A hub sends every piece of data to every device, wasting traffic
A hub needs fibre optic cables to work at all
q.why: Switches send data only to the right device.

q.q: Why might a desktop PC be connected by cable rather than Wi-Fi?
o: It is usually faster and more reliable
It only works on phones and tablets
You can walk around with your device
It needs no cables at all
q.why: Cables give a steady, fast connection.

q.q: Bluetooth is designed to work over roughly what distance?
o: About 10 metres
About 1 metre
About 1 kilometre
About 100 metres
q.why: Bluetooth is designed for short-range links.

q.q: Which job is Bluetooth best suited to?
o: Streaming 4K video to 30 laptops
Linking two schools together
Connecting wireless earbuds to a phone
Connecting a server to the school switch
q.why: Short range, low power, two devices.

q.q: Why should a Wi-Fi network have a password?
o: To make the connection run faster
To increase the range of the signal
So that Bluetooth devices can pair
To stop strangers joining and to encrypt the data
q.why: The key controls who can join and scrambles the data.

q.q: What is the typical indoor range of Wi-Fi?
o: Many kilometres
Unlimited
About 1 metre
A few tens of metres
q.why: The signal weakens through thick walls.

q.q: Why is Bluetooth perfect for small battery-powered gadgets?
o: It has a range of many kilometres
It is faster than Wi-Fi
It needs a cable to pair
It uses very little power
q.why: Low power suits earbuds and smartwatches.

q.q: Why are wireless connections less secure than wired ones?
o: Signals travel through the air and can be picked up nearby
Wireless data can never be encrypted by any device
Wireless devices do not have any MAC address
Anyone can plug a cable into a wireless network
q.why: So wireless data must be encrypted.

q.q: Your games console keeps lagging online over Wi-Fi. What do the notes suggest?
o: Plug it straight into the router with an Ethernet cable
Connect it to the router using Bluetooth instead
Move it further away from the router to reduce noise
Turn off the router's Wi-Fi password to speed it up
q.why: A wired link is usually faster and steadier.

q.q: Why should you avoid logging in to a bank account on free café Wi-Fi?
o: It is always much too slow
It is often not encrypted
It changes your MAC address
It uses Bluetooth instead
q.why: Others nearby could read unencrypted data.

q.q: In a star network, what does every computer's cable connect to?
o: A printer
A modem
A terminator
A switch
q.why: Every device has its own cable to the central switch.

q.q: What happens in a bus network if the backbone cable breaks?
o: Data takes another route
Nothing happens at all
The whole network fails
Only one computer is affected
q.why: Every device relies on the single backbone.

q.q: Why is a mesh network very reliable?
o: It has a central switch that never fails
It uses only one cable for all of its devices
There are many routes, so data can go around a broken link
It only works with Bluetooth connections
q.why: There is no single point of failure.

q.q: The internet is best described as which topology?
o: Mesh
Bus
Star
Peer-to-peer
q.why: The internet is a huge partial mesh of routers.

q.q: What is a topology?
o: The address of a device
The shape or layout of a network
The speed of a network
The rules for sending data
q.why: It describes how devices are connected.

q.q: In a star network, one computer's cable breaks. What happens?
o: The whole network fails straight away
Data collides on the backbone cable
The central switch stops working too
Only that one computer loses its connection
q.why: Everyone else carries on.

q.q: What is the main disadvantage of a star topology?
o: If one cable breaks, the whole network goes down
If the central switch fails, the whole network goes down
Every device can see all of the data
Only one device can send data at a time
q.why: The switch is a single point of failure.

q.q: In a bus network, what is the job of a terminator?
o: To send data only to the right device
To stop signals bouncing back at each end
To connect the network to the internet
To give each device an IP address
q.why: There is a terminator at each end of the backbone.

q.q: Why does a bus network slow down as more devices are added?
o: Each new device needs its own switch
Only one device can send at a time, so data collides
The terminators use up the bandwidth
The backbone gets shorter with each device
q.why: Collisions make it slower.

q.q: How many cables does a full mesh of 4 devices need?
q.why: Each pair needs one link: 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6.

q.q: How many cables does a full mesh of 5 devices need?
In a client-server network, what is a client?
o: A cable that links two networks together
A computer that requests services from a server
A network that has no central server
A computer that provides services to others
q.why: Clients ask; servers provide.

q.q: In which network model is every computer equal, with no central server?
o: Peer-to-peer
Star
WAN
Client-server
q.why: In P2P every computer is equal.

q.q: Why does a school use a client-server network?
o: It does not need a technician to look after it
It is the cheapest option for a large school
It lets every pupil share files directly with others
Logins, security and backups can be managed centrally
q.why: Central control suits hundreds of users.

q.q: Which server checks your username and password when you log on?
o: Authentication server
Print server
Web server
Email server
q.why: Authentication means checking who you are.

q.q: Which server manages a queue of print jobs for shared printers?
o: Authentication server
File server
Web server
Print server
q.why: It handles printing in the computer room.

q.q: Two friends send photos straight to each other's phones with AirDrop. Which model is this?
o: WAN
Client-server
Peer-to-peer
Star topology
q.why: There is no server: the devices share directly.

q.q: In a peer-to-peer network, who backs up the files?
o: The technician backs up everything centrally
Each user must back up their own computer
The server backs up every peer automatically
The router keeps a copy of every file
q.why: There is no central server in P2P.

q.q: Which is best for a family with two laptops at home?
o: Peer-to-peer, because it is cheap and simple
Client-server, because it is the cheapest
Peer-to-peer, because it is easiest to secure
Client-server, because it needs a technician
q.why: P2P suits homes and very small offices.

q.q: When you visit a website, what is your browser acting as?
o: A client
A switch
A peer
A server
q.why: The computer storing the website is the web server.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of a client-server network?
o: Security is harder to control
There is no central place to store files
Each user must back up their own files
It is expensive, needing servers and a technician
q.why: The other options describe peer-to-peer.

q.q: Where in a packet would a router find the destination IP address?
o: The header
The payload
The trailer
The router
q.why: The header is like the address label on a parcel.

q.q: Why might packets arrive in the wrong order?
o: Wi-Fi reverses the order of packets
Packets do not have any numbers
They are sent by different routes
The computer receiving them is broken
q.why: Some routes are quicker than others.

q.q: What happens if a packet goes missing?
o: The whole file is deleted and must be resent
The router keeps the packet forever
All the other packets are thrown away
The receiver asks for that packet to be sent again
q.why: Only the missing packet is resent.

q.q: TCP/IP and HTTPS are protocols. What is a protocol?
o: A program that spreads across networks
A set of rules for how devices communicate
A very fast type of router
A type of cable used in networks
q.why: Everyone follows the same rules.

q.q: What is the payload of a packet?
o: The actual piece of data being sent
The sender's and receiver's addresses
A check value to spot damage
The marker for the end of the packet
q.why: The payload is the contents of the box.

q.q: What does the trailer of a packet contain?
o: A check value to spot damage and an end marker
The name of the website being visited
The actual piece of photo or message data
The sender's and destination IP addresses
q.why: It is like a seal on a parcel.

q.q: How does the receiving computer put packets back in the right order?
o: It sorts them by the size of their payload
It uses the MAC address of each router
It asks the sender to resend them all in order
It uses the packet numbers in the headers
q.why: Each packet is numbered, e.g. 3 of 50.

q.q: What does a router do with each packet it receives?
o: Stores it until the whole file has arrived
Sends it back to the sender to check it
Reads the destination address and sends it on by the best route
Opens the payload and checks the photo is correct
q.why: The best route at that moment is chosen.

q.q: Which part of TCP/IP splits data into packets, numbers them and checks they all arrive?
o: HTTP
IP
TCP
DNS
q.why: IP handles addressing and routing.

q.q: Why is packet switching efficient?
o: Many users can share the same cables, with packets taking turns
Each user gets their own private cable to the internet
Packets never need to be resent if damaged
Every packet always takes exactly the same route
q.why: Packets from different users share the links.

q.q: One packet of a large photo is damaged. What has to be resent?
o: Half of the photo
Only the damaged packet
Every packet after it
The whole photo
q.why: Only damaged parts are resent.

q.q: Which is a valid IPv4 address?
q.why: Four numbers, each 0 to 255.

q.q: Where does a device's MAC address come from?
o: It is looked up from a DNS server
It is given out by the router when you join
It is built into the NIC when it is made
It is set by the web server you visit
q.why: The manufacturer builds it into the network interface card.

q.q: What was the main reason for introducing IPv6?
o: IPv4 addresses were too slow to use
The world was running out of IPv4 addresses
To make Bluetooth work over long distances
To replace MAC addresses completely
q.why: IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion addresses.

q.q: Your phone connects to Wi-Fi at school, then at home. What happens?
o: Both its IP address and its MAC address change to new ones
Its IP address will probably change but its MAC address stays the same
Its MAC address will change but its IP address stays the same
Both its IP address and its MAC address stay exactly the same
q.why: IP addresses depend on the network; MAC addresses are fixed.

q.q: Why is 192.168.1.256 not a valid IPv4 address?
o: It has too many dots
It does not use letters
256 is bigger than 255
It starts with 192
q.why: Each number must be from 0 to 255.

q.q: How is a MAC address written?
o: Eight letters and a dot
12 hexadecimal digits in pairs
A domain name such as bbc.co.uk
Four numbers from 0 to 255

q.q: Which device uses MAC addresses to send data within a LAN?
o: DNS server
Switch
Router
Modem
q.why: Routers use IP addresses between networks.

q.q: In the name and address comparison, the MAC address is like your...
o: name, which stays with you wherever you go
phone number, which you can choose
postal address, which changes if you move
password, which you should change often
q.why: The IP address is like your postal address.

q.q: Who usually gives a device its IP address on a home network?
o: The manufacturer
The DNS server
The web server
The router
q.why: MAC addresses come from the manufacturer.

q.q: Which IP address is most likely to be a private address inside a home?
q.why: Private addresses often start 192.168 or 10.

q.q: What is the main job of DNS?
o: Stores all the web pages in the world
Translates domain names into IP addresses
Gives each device its MAC address
Speeds up your Wi-Fi connection
q.why: It is the internet's phone book.

q.q: In https://www.ergs.org/sport, which part is the path?
o: https://
ergs.org
/sport
www.
q.why: The path picks the page on the web server.

q.q: What does the browser do after it receives the IP address from DNS?
o: Turns off the Wi-Fi to save power while it waits
Asks the DNS server for the same IP address again
Sends a request for the page to the web server at that address
Deletes its cache so the page is fresh
q.why: Now it knows where the website lives.

q.q: Why does a website you visit often load faster?
o: The page is sent using Bluetooth instead
Your MAC address changes to a faster one
The website remembers your name and sends it first
The IP address is cached, so the DNS lookup can be skipped
q.why: Caching saves the lookup step.

q.q: In https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport, which part is the domain name?
o: www.
bbc.co.uk
/sport
https://
q.why: DNS turns the domain name into an IP address.

q.q: What does the s in https:// mean?
o: The site is a sports site
The page is small
The server is in Scotland
The connection is secure (encrypted)
q.why: HTTPS is the secure protocol.

q.q: What does URL stand for?
o: Universal Router Link
Uniform Remote Login
User Request Line
Uniform Resource Locator
q.why: The URL is the whole web address.

q.q: DNS servers are down but your internet connection is fine. What happens?
o: Websites will not load by name
Every website loads normally
Your MAC address is lost
Your Wi-Fi password stops working
q.why: It can look as if the internet is down.

q.q: Why do people use domain names rather than IP addresses?
o: Domain names make pages load faster
Computers cannot understand IP addresses
Names are easier for people to remember
IP addresses are kept secret
q.why: Computers use IP addresses; people use names.

q.q: Why do DNS servers ask each other for addresses?
o: No single DNS server knows every domain name
Web servers block DNS requests
Each DNS server only works for one hour
DNS servers cannot store numbers
q.why: Together they hold the whole directory.

q.q: Broadband speeds are given in Mbps. What does Mbps stand for?
o: Megabits per second
Megabytes per second
Maximum bits per signal
Million bytes per screen
q.why: Small b = bits.

q.q: A 100 MB file is downloaded at 20 Mbps. How long does it take?
o: 20 seconds
80 seconds
40 seconds
5 seconds

q.q: Why do you multiply a file size in MB by 8?
o: Because there are 8 routers on the way
To turn seconds into minutes
To add the size of the packet headers
To turn megabytes into megabits
q.why: There are 8 bits in every byte.

q.q: Which matters most for a fast-paced online game?
o: A big monitor
A long MAC address
Large storage
Low latency
q.why: Actions must reach the server with little delay.

q.q: What is bandwidth?
o: The maximum amount of data that can be sent each second
The delay before any data starts to arrive
The distance that a Wi-Fi signal can reach
The number of devices connected to a network
q.why: Like the number of lanes on a motorway.

q.q: A 50 MB file is downloaded at 10 Mbps. How long does it take?
o: 50 seconds
5 seconds
400 seconds
40 seconds

q.q: A 2 GB game is downloaded at 100 Mbps (use 1 GB = 1000 MB). How long does it take?
o: 160 seconds
2,000 seconds
20 seconds
1,600 seconds

q.q: A 300 MB file downloads at 40 Mbps. How long does it take?
o: 120 seconds
60 seconds
75 seconds
7.5 seconds

q.q: What is latency?
o: The maximum data sent each second
The number of packets in a file
The delay before data starts to arrive
The size of a file in megabytes
q.why: Measured in milliseconds; also called ping or lag.

q.q: Why do real downloads usually take longer than the calculation says?
o: The connection may be shared and packets carry extra header data
Each byte is split into 16 bits during a download
Downloads always use Bluetooth for part of the way
Calculations always round the file size down to zero
q.why: The calculation is a best case.

q.q: Which of these stores your files in the cloud?
o: A DVD
The hard drive in your PC
OneDrive
A USB memory stick
q.why: OneDrive stores your files on Microsoft's servers.

q.q: What is the main disadvantage of cloud storage?
o: You can open your files from any device
You need an internet connection to access your files
Your files are backed up if your laptop breaks
It is easy to share files with other people
q.why: No connection, no files.

q.q: Which of these devices is part of the Internet of Things?
o: A paper diary kept in your school bag
A printed library book with a barcode
A pencil with a rubber on the end
A smart thermostat controlled from your phone
q.why: It has sensors and an internet connection.

q.q: Why is it risky to leave a smart device on its default password?
o: It makes the device use far more electricity
It makes the device run much more slowly
Default passwords are widely known, so hackers can get in
It stops Bluetooth devices from pairing
q.why: Change it to a strong, unique password.

q.q: Where are the servers that make up 'the cloud'?
o: Inside your own laptop
In data centres owned by big companies
Floating in the sky above us
In your home router
q.why: You reach them over the internet.

q.q: What is the Internet of Things?
o: All of the websites stored on web servers worldwide
A list of every device's MAC address on the internet
Everyday objects with sensors and an internet connection
The undersea cables that link countries together
q.why: Smart devices collect and share data.

q.q: Which is a privacy risk of IoT devices?
o: They can only be used if you also pay for cloud storage
They collect personal data such as who is home and what you say
They stop all the other devices from using the internet
They make every website in the home load more slowly
q.why: Devices collect lots of personal data.

q.q: How can you protect a cloud account even if someone guesses your password?
o: Turn off encryption
Turn on two-factor authentication
Share the password with a friend
Use a shorter password
q.why: They would still need the code from your phone.

q.q: Why does cloud storage help a pupil with homework?
o: They no longer need any internet connection
It makes every file smaller to download
They can start work in school and finish it at home
It stops the teacher from seeing their work
q.why: Files can be opened from any device.
